title: Random Signals and Noise
tagline: Probability for engineers, random processes, correlation and power spectra, noise and optimal filtering
summary: Noise limits every measurement and every communication link. This course reviews probability for engineers and develops random processes: stationarity, correlation functions and power spectral densities, random signals in linear systems, Gaussian and thermal noise, and the matched, Wiener and Kalman filters that extract signals from noise.
overview: Every measurement and every communication link is limited by **noise**: the thermal agitation of electrons in a resistor, the granularity of current crossing a junction, the rounding error of a converter, the interference of other users. Noise cannot be predicted sample by sample, yet its averages — its mean, its power, the way that power is spread over frequency — are as stable and measurable as a resistance. This course develops the theory that makes such statements precise and turns them into design numbers: how many bits a converter really resolves, how far a radar can see, how many errors a receiver makes, and how much a filter can clean up a signal.

The course begins with **probability for engineers** — random variables, the Gaussian and its $Q$-function, joint distributions and functions of random variables — and then moves from numbers to waveforms with **random processes**, stationarity and ergodicity. The central chapters describe a stationary process by its **autocorrelation** and its **power spectral density**, linked by the Wiener–Khinchin theorem, and show what an LTI system does to them: the output spectrum is $\abs{H}^2$ times the input spectrum, the most used result in the theory of noise. With these tools we model **thermal and shot noise** and band-pass noise from physics, and finish with the optimal linear processors that extract signals from noise: the **matched filter**, the **Wiener filter**, least squares and the **Kalman filter**.

The subject is hard mainly because two kinds of average must be kept apart: the ensemble average over all possible waveforms, which the theory uses, and the time average over the one recording that an engineer actually has; ergodicity is the bridge between them. A second difficulty is bookkeeping — one-sided versus two-sided spectra, $N_0$ versus $N_0/2$, power versus amplitude, hertz versus radians per second. Work each result through a concrete example with numbers, check it with a short simulation, and keep track of the units of every spectral density.
outcomes: Compute probabilities, means, variances and error probabilities for discrete, continuous and Gaussian random variables, using the $Q$-function where needed.
Describe pairs of random variables by joint distributions, covariance and the correlation coefficient, and find the distribution of a function of random variables.
Classify random processes as stationary, wide-sense stationary or ergodic, and compute the mean and autocorrelation of the standard processes.
Derive the Wiener–Khinchin theorem and compute power spectral densities and cross-spectra, including the spectrum of a random binary data signal.
Calculate the output mean, autocorrelation and spectrum of an LTI system driven by a random input, and use the noise-equivalent bandwidth.
Model thermal and shot noise from first principles, and analyse band-pass noise through its in-phase and quadrature components and its Rayleigh envelope.
Derive the matched filter and the Wiener filter, and evaluate the signal-to-noise ratio and mean-square error they achieve.
Formulate and solve least-squares and minimum mean-square-error estimation problems, and design a discrete Kalman filter for a linear state-space model.
Verify noise calculations by simulating random signals and estimating their statistics and spectra from data.

history.title: The law of errors and least squares
history.detail: In Theoria motus Carl Friedrich Gauss derived the normal distribution as the law of observational errors and justified the method of least squares, which Adrien-Marie Legendre had published in 1805.

history.title: Brownian motion
history.detail: Albert Einstein's analysis of Brownian motion, followed by Marian Smoluchowski's in 1906, treated a physical random process quantitatively and predicted that mean-square displacement grows linearly with time.

history.title: Shot noise predicted
history.detail: Walter Schottky showed that the discreteness of electronic charge makes the current of a vacuum tube fluctuate, with a mean-square value proportional to the current and the bandwidth.

history.title: Thermal noise measured and explained
history.detail: John B. Johnson reported measurements of the noise voltage of resistors at Bell Laboratories, and Harry Nyquist derived its spectral density $4kTR$ from thermodynamics in a companion paper in Physical Review.

history.title: Generalised harmonic analysis
history.detail: Norbert Wiener's paper in Acta Mathematica related the autocorrelation of a function to its power spectrum; Aleksandr Khinchin proved the corresponding theorem for stationary random processes in 1934.

history.title: Axioms of probability
history.detail: Andrey Kolmogorov's Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung founded probability on measure theory, the basis on which the theory of random processes was built.

history.title: The matched filter
history.detail: Dwight O. North at RCA Laboratories derived the filter that maximises the signal-to-noise ratio of a known pulse in noise, in a classified report on radar detection.

history.title: Mathematical analysis of random noise
history.detail: Stephen O. Rice's two-part paper in the Bell System Technical Journal (1944–45) set out the statistics of filtered Gaussian noise, band-pass noise and the envelope of a sinusoid plus noise.

history.title: Wiener's filtering theory published
history.detail: Norbert Wiener's wartime report on optimal prediction and filtering of stationary time series appeared as the book Extrapolation, Interpolation, and Smoothing of Stationary Time Series.

history.title: The Kalman filter
history.detail: Rudolf E. Kálmán published a recursive solution of the linear filtering problem in state-space form; with Richard Bucy he gave the continuous-time version in 1961.

references.title: Probability, Random Variables and Stochastic Processes (4th ed.)
references.note: The classic engineering text on probability and random processes; thorough on correlation, spectra and linear systems.

references.title: Probability and Random Processes for Electrical and Computer Engineers
references.note: A careful, modern undergraduate text with many worked problems on random variables, processes and estimation.

references.title: Probability, Statistics, and Random Processes for Electrical Engineering (3rd ed.)
references.note: Accessible and example-rich, with good chapters on random signals in linear systems and on Markov chains.

references.title: Probabilistic Methods of Signal and System Analysis (3rd ed.)
references.authors: George R. Cooper, Clare D. McGillem
references.note: A gentle introduction aimed at signals courses, strong on noise in systems and on the noise-equivalent bandwidth.

references.title: Communication Systems (4th ed.)
references.note: Its chapters on random processes, band-pass noise and the matched filter show the theory at work in receivers.

references.title: Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing, Volume I: Estimation Theory
references.note: The standard reference for least squares, MMSE estimation and the Kalman filter, with clear derivations.

references.title: Low-Noise Electronic System Design
references.authors: C. D. Motchenbacher, J. A. Connelly
references.note: Thermal, shot and flicker noise in real components and circuits, for readers who want to apply the noise models to hardware.
